Compare the resulting expression term-by-term against the full model's expected time using the fact that the full model minimizes certain overlap statistics while the projective plane maximizes them.     `1 - ∑ f i ≤ ∏ (1 - f i)`.  Proved by induction; the inductive step needs
    both `0 ≤ ∏` and `∏ ≤ 1`. -/
theorem one_sub_sum_le_prod_one_sub (s : Finset ℕ) (f : ℕ → ℚ)
    (h : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ f i ∧ f i ≤ 1) :
    1 - ∑ i ∈ s, f i ≤ ∏ i ∈ s, (1 - f i) := by
  classical
  induction s using Finset.induction with
  | empty => simp
  | @insert a s ha ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_insert ha, Finset.prod_insert ha]
      have hb := h a (Finset.mem_insert_self a s)
      have ih' := ih (fun i hi => h i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hi))
      have hprod_nonneg : 0 ≤ ∏ i ∈ s, (1 - f i) :=
        Finset.prod_nonneg (fun i hi => by
          have := (h i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hi)).2; linarith)
      have hprod_le_one : ∏ i ∈ s, (1 - f i) ≤ 1 :=
        Finset.prod_le_one
          (fun i hi => by have := (h i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hi)).2; linarith)
          (fun i hi => by have := (h i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hi)).1; linarith)
      nlinarith [hb.1, hb.2, ih', hprod_nonneg, hprod_le_one]

/-- The exact probability that `q` uniform independent queries into `n` slots are
    all distinct: `n^{\underline q}/n^q` where `n^{\underline q}` is the
    descending factorial (the number of injective assignments). -/
noncomputable def noCollisionProb (n q : ℕ) : ℚ :=
  (n.descFactorial q : ℚ) / (n : ℚ) ^ q

/-- **Exact collision-free count.** The number of injective (collision-free)
    assignments of `q` queries into `n` slots is the descending factorial
    `n.descFactorial q`. -/
theorem card_injective_assignments (n q : ℕ) :
    Fintype.card (Fin q ↪ Fin n) = n.descFactorial q := by
  simp [Fintype.card_embedding_eq]

/-- Gauss sum, cast to `ℚ`: `∑_{i<q} i = q(q-1)/2`. -/
theorem sum_range_cast (q : ℕ) : (∑ i ∈ range q, (i : ℚ)) = (q * (q - 1) : ℚ) / 2 := by
  rcases q with _ | m
  · simp
  · have h2 := Finset.sum_range_id_mul_two (m + 1)
    have hc := congrArg (Nat.cast (R := ℚ)) h2
    push_cast at hc ⊢
    linarith [hc]

/-- **Exact no-collision probability as a product.** For `q ≤ n`,
    `noCollisionProb n q = ∏_{i<q} (1 - i/n)`. -/
theorem noCollisionProb_eq_prod (n q : ℕ) (hq : q ≤ n) :
    noCollisionProb n q = ∏ i ∈ range q, (1 - (i : ℚ) / n) := by
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos n with hn | hn
  · subst hn; interval_cases q; simp [noCollisionProb]
  · have hn' : (n : ℚ) ≠ 0 := by positivity
    have hRHS : ∏ i ∈ range q, (1 - (i : ℚ) / n)
        = (∏ i ∈ range q, ((n : ℚ) - i)) / (n : ℚ) ^ q := by
      rw [Finset.prod_congr rfl
        (fun i _ => by field_simp : ∀ i ∈ range q, (1 - (i : ℚ) / n) = ((n : ℚ) - i) / n)]
      rw [Finset.prod_div_distrib, Finset.prod_const, Finset.card_range]
    rw [hRHS]; unfold noCollisionProb
    rw [Nat.descFactorial_eq_prod_range]; push_cast
    congr 1
    apply Finset.prod_congr rfl
    intro i hi
    rw [mem_range] at hi
    rw [Nat.cast_sub (by omega)]

/-- **Birthday pigeonhole.** Once the number of queries exceeds the digest space
    (`q > n`), a collision is unavoidable: some two distinct queries hash equal. -/
theorem birthday_pigeonhole (n q : ℕ) (hqn : n < q) (f : Fin q → Fin n) :
    ∃ i j, i ≠ j ∧ f i = f j := by
  apply Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt
  simpa using hqn

/-- **The birthday bound.** For `q ≤ n` queries into an `n`-element digest space,
    the probability of at least one collision is at most `q(q-1)/(2n)`.  This is
    the quantitative ceiling on collision resistance: to reach `b`-bit security
    (`q ≈ 2^b` queries safe) the digest space must satisfy `n ≈ 2^{2b}`. -/
theorem birthday_collision_bound (n q : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) (hq : q ≤ n) :
    1 - noCollisionProb n q ≤ (q * (q - 1) : ℚ) / (2 * n) := by
  have hn' : (0 : ℚ) < n := by exact_mod_cast hn
  rw [noCollisionProb_eq_prod n q hq]
  have hWeier : 1 - ∑ i ∈ range q, ((i : ℚ) / n) ≤ ∏ i ∈ range q, (1 - (i : ℚ) / n) := by
    apply one_sub_sum_le_prod_one_sub
    intro i hi
    rw [mem_range] at hi
    exact ⟨by positivity, by rw [div_le_one hn']; exact_mod_cast (by omega : i ≤ n)⟩
  have hsum : ∑ i ∈ range q, ((i : ℚ) / n) = (q * (q - 1) : ℚ) / (2 * n) := by
    rw [← Finset.sum_div, sum_range_cast]; ring
  linarith [hWeier, hsum.ge]

end Cryptography.Birthday

/-
  Merkle *Tree* Collision-Resistance Preservation
  ===============================================

  The Merkle–Damgård construction (see `Cryptography.MerkleDamgard`) iterates a
  compression function *linearly* along a message.  The other canonical domain
  extender is the **Merkle tree**: a two-to-one compression function `h` is
  applied along a *binary tree*, hashing pairs of chaining values up to a single
  root.  Merkle trees underlie authenticated data structures, certificate
  transparency, and blockchains, and — like the linear chain — they *preserve
  collision resistance*.

  We prove the tree analogue of `md_collision_extract`: any collision of the tree
  hash on two trees of the **same shape** constructively yields a collision of
  the underlying two-input compression function `h`.  The proof is a structural
  induction over the common shape, splitting each internal node into "the two
  child digests already collide" versus "recurse into the differing subtree".

  This complements the linear result: collision resistance is preserved by *both*
  the sequential (MD) and the parallel (tree) domain extenders, from the *same*
  primitive assumption (`HasPairCollision`, the two-input version of
  `Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.HasCompressionCollision`).

  -- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
  HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer): Collision resistance is preserved by the Merkle
  *tree* extender exactly as for the linear chain: a root collision on same-shape
  trees must be traceable to a two-input compression collision at some internal
  node.

  EXPERIMENT (Experimenter): Introduced `MTree`, `treeHash`, and a `SameShape`
  relation making the two trees structurally comparable.  `tree_collision_extract`
  is proved by induction on `SameShape`.  At an internal node either the pair of
  child digests already differs (immediate `HasPairCollision`), or the digests
  agree and, since the trees differ, a differing subtree is found by the IH.

  ANALYSIS (Analyst): The `SameShape` hypothesis is the tree analogue of the
  equal-length hypothesis in the linear case: without it, two structurally
  different trees can share a root without any node collision (e.g. a leaf whose
  value equals the root hash of a subtree).  The theorem is stated at that tight
  boundary.  Injectivity is not assumed: the reduction is purely extractive.

  CRITIQUE (Critic): Non-vacuity — `treeHash_injOn_shape` shows the contrapositive
  (no `h`-collision ⇒ tree hash injective on each shape), and `pair_collision_of_card`
  proves via pigeonhole that two-input compressions over a ≥2-element finite state
  always *have* a collision, so the extraction theorem is about *finding*, not
  *existence*.  The base case genuinely uses `hne` (equal leaves are equal trees).

  SYNTHESIS (PI): `MTree` + `treeHash` + `SameShape` + `tree_collision_extract`
  + injectivity corollary + pigeonhole inevitability form a self-contained
  Merkle-*tree* collision-resistance package, parallel to the Merkle–Damgård one.
-/
import Mathlib
import Cryptography.MerkleDamgard

namespace Cryptography.MerkleTree

variable {State : Type*}

/-- A binary Merkle tree with `State`-labelled leaves. -/
inductive MTree (State : Type*) where
  | leaf : State → MTree State
  | node : MTree State → MTree State → MTree State

/-- The Merkle tree hash: leaves carry their value, internal nodes apply the
    two-to-one compression function `h` to the digests of their two children. -/
def treeHash (h : State → State → State) : MTree State → State
  | .leaf s => s
  | .node l r => h (treeHash h l) (treeHash h r)

/-- A two-input compression function `h` has a *collision* when two distinct
    input pairs `(a,b) ≠ (c,d)` map to the same output.  This is the two-argument
    analogue of `Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.HasCompressionCollision`. -/
def HasPairCollision (h : State → State → State) : Prop :=
  ∃ a b c d, (a, b) ≠ (c, d) ∧ h a b = h c d

/-- Two trees have the *same shape* when their branching structure matches,
    ignoring leaf values. -/
inductive SameShape : MTree State → MTree State → Prop
  | leaf (s t : State) : SameShape (.leaf s) (.leaf t)
  | node {l₁ r₁ l₂ r₂ : MTree State} :
      SameShape l₁ l₂ → SameShape r₁ r₂ →
      SameShape (.node l₁ r₁) (.node l₂ r₂)

@[simp] theorem treeHash_leaf (h : State → State → State) (s : State) :
    treeHash h (.leaf s) = s := rfl

@[simp] theorem treeHash_node (h : State → State → State) (l r : MTree State) :
    treeHash h (.node l r) = h (treeHash h l) (treeHash h r) := rfl

/-- `SameShape` is reflexive. -/
theorem SameShape.refl (t : MTree State) : SameShape t t := by
  induction t with
  | leaf s => exact SameShape.leaf s s
  | node l r ihl ihr => exact SameShape.node ihl ihr

/-- **Merkle-tree collision extraction.**
    Any collision of the tree hash on two distinct, *same-shape* trees yields an
    explicit collision of the two-input compression function `h`. -/
theorem tree_collision_extract (h : State → State → State)
    (t₁ t₂ : MTree State) (hshape : SameShape t₁ t₂) (hne : t₁ ≠ t₂)
    (hcol : treeHash h t₁ = treeHash h t₂) :
    HasPairCollision h := by
  induction hshape with
  | leaf s t =>
      simp only [treeHash] at hcol
      exact absurd (by rw [hcol]) hne
  | @node l₁ r₁ l₂ r₂ hl hr ihl ihr =>
      simp only [treeHash] at hcol
      by_cases hpair : (treeHash h l₁, treeHash h r₁) = (treeHash h l₂, treeHash h r₂)
      · rw [Prod.mk.injEq] at hpair
        obtain ⟨hlh, hrh⟩ := hpair
        by_cases hll : l₁ = l₂
        · by_cases hrr : r₁ = r₂
          · exact absurd (by rw [hll, hrr]) hne
          · exact ihr hrr hrh
        · exact ihl hll hlh
      · exact ⟨_, _, _, _, hpair, hcol⟩

/-- **Collision resistance is preserved (contrapositive form).**
    If the compression function has no collision, then the tree hash is injective
    on each fixed tree shape. -/
theorem treeHash_injOn_shape (h : State → State → State)
    (hh : ¬ HasPairCollision h) (t₁ t₂ : MTree State)
    (hshape : SameShape t₁ t₂) (hcol : treeHash h t₁ = treeHash h t₂) :
    t₁ = t₂ := by
  by_contra hne
  exact hh (tree_collision_extract h t₁ t₂ hshape hne hcol)

/-- **Collisions are inevitable (pigeonhole).**
    A two-input compression function over a finite state space with at least two
    elements necessarily has a collision: its domain `State × State` is strictly
    larger than its codomain.  Collision resistance is therefore a *computational*
    notion — collisions exist; the difficulty is finding them. -/
theorem pair_collision_of_card [Fintype State] (hcard : 1 < Fintype.card State)
    (h : State → State → State) : HasPairCollision h := by
  have hpos : 0 < Fintype.card State := by omega
  obtain ⟨p, q, hpq, hval⟩ := Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt
    (fun p : State × State => h p.1 p.2)
    (by simpa [Fintype.card_prod] using
      (by nlinarith : Fintype.card State < Fintype.card State * Fintype.card State))
  exact ⟨p.1, p.2, q.1, q.2, by simpa using hpq, hval⟩

/-- **Both domain extenders start from an unavoidable collision.**
    Over finite state/block types (state with `≥ 2` elements, blocks with `≥ 2`
    values), the *linear* Merkle–Damgård compression `f` and the *tree* two-input
    compression `h` each necessarily have a collision.  This ties the tree
    inevitability (`pair_collision_of_card`) to the linear one
    (`Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.compression_collision_of_card`), showing both
    constructions rest on the *computational* (find-the-collision) hardness, not
    on collisions being absent. -/
theorem collisions_inevitable_both {Block : Type*}
    [Fintype State] [Fintype Block] [Nonempty State]
    (hcard : 1 < Fintype.card State) (hB : 1 < Fintype.card Block)
    (f : State → Block → State) (h : State → State → State) :
    Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.HasCompressionCollision f ∧ HasPairCollision h :=
  ⟨Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.compression_collision_of_card hB f,
   pair_collision_of_card hcard h⟩

end Cryptography.MerkleTree

# Computational Evidence — Collision Resistance of Hash Domain Extenders

This note collects the small-case numerical checks performed before formalizing
the two Lean files `MerkleTreeCollision.lean` and `BirthdayCollisionBound.lean`.

## 1. Birthday bound: exact no-collision probability vs. the quadratic upper bound

For a random function into `n` slots queried `q` times, the exact no-collision
probability is `P_nc(n,q) = ∏_{i<q} (1 - i/n)` and the collision probability is
`1 - P_nc`. The formalized bound is `1 - P_nc ≤ q(q-1)/(2n)`.

Classic `n = 365` (the actual "birthday paradox"):

| q  | P_nc     | collision prob = 1 − P_nc | bound q(q−1)/(2·365) |
|----|----------|---------------------------|----------------------|
| 10 | 0.883052 | 0.116948                  | 0.123288             |
| 20 | 0.588562 | 0.411438                  | 0.520548             |
| 22 | 0.524305 | 0.475695                  | 0.632877             |
| 23 | 0.492703 | 0.507297                  | 0.693151             |
| 29 | 0.319031 | 0.680969                  | 1.112329             |

Observations:
- The collision probability first exceeds `1/2` at `q = 23` (0.5073), the
  textbook birthday number — a sanity check on `noCollisionProb_eq_prod`.
- The upper bound `q(q-1)/(2n)` dominates the true collision probability at every
  `q` in the table (e.g. `q=2`: `0.002740 ≥ 0.002740`, tight; `q=23`:
  `0.693 ≥ 0.507`), consistent with `birthday_collision_bound`.
- For `q > n` the product contains a zero factor, so `P_nc = 0`: a collision is
  certain. This is the qualitative statement proved by `birthday_pigeonhole`.

## 2. Exact collision-free counts (descending factorial)

The number of collision-free assignments of `q` queries into `n` slots equals
`n^{\underline q} = n·(n−1)···(n−q+1)`, formalized as `card (Fin q ↪ Fin n) =
n.descFactorial q`. For `n = 10`:

`descFactorial 10 q` for `q = 0..5`: `1, 10, 90, 720, 5040, 30240`.

These are the falling factorials of 10 — **OEIS A008279** (triangle of
`n!/(n−k)!`, arrangements/permutations of `n` things `k` at a time). The `n = 10`
row matches A008279 exactly, confirming the exact-count formalization.

## 3. Merkle-tree collision extraction — hand-checked small cases

Two same-shape trees over a toy compression `h a b = (a + b) mod 4` on
`State = ZMod 4`:

- `t₁ = node (leaf 0) (leaf 3)`, `t₂ = node (leaf 1) (leaf 2)`.
  Root hashes: `h 0 3 = 3` and `h 1 2 = 3` — equal, trees differ, and
  `(0,3) ≠ (1,2)` is a genuine pair collision of `h`. This is exactly the
  "digests already differ at the root" branch of `tree_collision_extract`.
- `t₁ = node (node (leaf 0) (leaf 1)) (leaf 3)`,
  `t₂ = node (node (leaf 2) (leaf 3)) (leaf 3)` with `h a b = (a+b) mod 4`:
  left subtree digests `h 0 1 = 1`, `h 2 3 = 1` collide while the right leaves
  match, illustrating the "recurse into the differing subtree" branch.

## 4. Inevitability (pigeonhole)

For any `h : State → State → State` with `|State| = m ≥ 2`, the domain
`State × State` has `m² > m` elements, so `h` cannot be injective and a pair
collision always exists (`pair_collision_of_card`). E.g. `m = 2`: `4 > 2`.
This confirms collision resistance is a *computational* (find-the-collision)
notion, never an information-theoretic absence of collisions.

All four checks are consistent with the formalized theorems; no counterexamples
were found in the sampled ranges.

# Future Directions — Collision Resistance of Hash Domain Extenders

This cycle established, with fully verified proofs, three complementary faces of
collision resistance for iterated hashing: the *linear* Merkle–Damgård extractor,
the *parallel* Merkle-tree extractor, and the *quantitative* birthday ceiling that
bounds any hash with a finite digest. The conjectures below are the natural next
steps suggested by that work. Each is stated so that a single decisive example or
counterexample would settle it.

## 1. A universal extraction law for tree-shaped domain extenders

**Conjecture.** Every domain extender built by applying a fixed two-input
compression function along an *arbitrary* directed acyclic combining schedule
(not only balanced binary trees, but skew trees, Merkle–Patricia tries, and
sponge-like absorbing graphs) preserves collision resistance: any collision on
two inputs sharing the same combining schedule can be traced, in time linear in
the schedule size, to a collision of the compression function.

The key insight is that collision extraction is a purely *local* property of the
combining graph — a root collision must be witnessed at some internal node where
two distinct digest pairs meet — so the same node-by-node descent that works for
balanced trees should work for any acyclic schedule, with the schedule playing
the role that "equal length" and "same shape" play in the linear and binary-tree
cases.

Why now? Modern authenticated data structures (certificate-transparency logs,
blockchain state tries, verkle trees) use exactly these irregular combining
schedules, yet their collision-resistance guarantees are argued informally per
construction; a single graph-level theorem would cover them uniformly.

## 2. The shape hypothesis is exactly necessary

**Conjecture.** For the binary Merkle-tree hash there is a sharp dichotomy: two
inputs of the *same* shape collide only via a compression collision, but for
every compression function that is not injective in its combined argument there
exist two *different-shaped* trees that collide with **no** internal compression
collision at all. In other words, "same shape" is not a convenience hypothesis —
it is the precise boundary of extractability.

compared against a bare leaf value, so the collision can be absorbed entirely by
the shape ambiguity rather than by any pair of equal compression outputs; making
the extender safe therefore requires domain separation that encodes shape (length
and branching) into the input, mirroring the prefix-free padding that repairs the
linear construction.

the classic Merkle–Damgård length-extension to tree-hash confusion in signature
schemes) keep re-appearing; pinning down that shape-encoding is *necessary and
sufficient* would turn a folklore rule of thumb into a design invariant.

structure can cluster collisions but cannot increase their expected count.

structure affects only the variance, i.e. how collisions bunch together, not
their mean.

differential collision attacks steer inputs along algebraic paths); separating
the "mean is structure-free" phenomenon from the "variance is structure-driven"
phenomenon would sharpen both attack analysis and provable-security margins.

**Conjecture.** The birthday bound is asymptotically tight in the strongest

`b`-bit-security rule a theorem rather than a heuristic.

competing cost pressures; a tight two-sided law converting output size directly
into an achievable security level would remove guesswork from those choices.

# Algebraic Theory of L-Function Germs

This module formalizes the algebraic theory of *germs* of L-functions at `s = 1`,
providing the structural results that underlie the analytic side of the
Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer (BSD) conjecture framework.

An L-function germ is modelled by the Taylor data of `L(s)` at `s = 1`, i.e. a
sequence of real coefficients `coeffs n` so that (formally)
`L(s) = ∑ n, coeffs n * (s - 1) ^ n`, together with a radius-of-convergence
guarantee.  The two invariants of central interest are:

* the **analytic rank** — the order of vanishing at `s = 1`, and
* the **leading coefficient** — the first nonzero Taylor coefficient.

The main structural results are that the analytic rank is *additive* and the
leading coefficient is *multiplicative* under the Rankin–Selberg style product
(the Cauchy product of Taylor coefficients).  These connect to the Selberg-class
degree bookkeeping in `Shared.SelbergClassCensus`.

## Notes on the statements

Two of the statements requested in the informal problem description are, taken
literally, *false*, and have been corrected here (the corrections are documented
at each theorem):

* `analyticRank_mul` requires non-vanishing hypotheses on `f` and `g`.
  Without them the all-zero germ (which has rank `0` by the degenerate
  convention) is a counterexample: if `f ≡ 0` and `g` has rank `3`, then
  `f · g ≡ 0` has rank `0 ≠ 0 + 3`.

* `selbergDegree_convolution` cannot hold as an *equality of degrees* with the
  convention `selbergDegree f = 2 * analyticRank f + 1`, because of a parity
  mismatch: `2·(r+s)+1 ≠ (2r+1)+(2s+1) = 2·(r+s)+2`.  The correct additive
  relation, proved below, is
  `selbergDegree (germMul f g) + 1 = selbergDegree f + selbergDegree g`.
-/

import Mathlib

open Finset BigOperators

open scoped Classical

namespace LFunctionGerm

/-- The germ of an L-function at `s = 1`, recorded through its Taylor data.

`coeffs n` is the `n`-th Taylor coefficient, so that formally
`L(s) = ∑ n, coeffs n * (s - 1) ^ n`. -/
structure _root_.LFunctionGerm where
  /-- The Taylor coefficients of `L` at `s = 1`. -/
  coeffs : ℕ → ℝ
  /-- Each coefficient is either zero or nonzero (a decidability witness used to
  extract the order of vanishing). -/
  wellDefined : ∀ n, coeffs n = 0 ∨ coeffs n ≠ 0
  /-- The Taylor series has a positive radius of convergence. -/
  converges : ∃ ε > 0, Summable (fun n => ‖coeffs n‖ * ε ^ n)

end LFunctionGerm

/-- A germ is *zero* when all of its Taylor coefficients vanish. -/
def LFunctionGerm.IsZero (f : LFunctionGerm) : Prop := ∀ n, f.coeffs n = 0

/--
A germ is nonzero iff it has some nonzero Taylor coefficient.
-/
theorem LFunctionGerm.not_isZero_iff (f : LFunctionGerm) :
    ¬ f.IsZero ↔ ∃ n, f.coeffs n ≠ 0 := by
  unfold LFunctionGerm.IsZero; aesop;

nonzero Taylor coefficient, or `0` for the degenerate all-zero germ. -/
noncomputable def analyticRank (f : LFunctionGerm) : ℕ :=
  if h : ∃ n, f.coeffs n ≠ 0 then Nat.find h else 0

/-- The **leading coefficient**: the first nonzero Taylor coefficient. -/
noncomputable def leadingCoeff (f : LFunctionGerm) : ℝ := f.coeffs (analyticRank f)

The leading Taylor coefficient of a product is the product of the leading

# Future Directions

Bold, testable conjectures distilled from this cycle's work on congruent numbers and
the analytic/arithmetic architecture of the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer formula.

## 1. A purely elementary certificate of non-congruence

**Conjecture.** For every squarefree positive integer `n` that is not a congruent
number, there is an explicit descent certificate — a finite, checkable collection of
local congruence conditions modulo a bounded modulus depending only on the squarefree
part of `n` — whose consistency is *equivalent* to non-congruence, and which never
appeals to the analytic behaviour of any L-function.

The key insight is that the passage "triangle → arithmetic progression of three
squares → rational point on `y² = x³ − n²x`" is completely reversible and unconditional,
so the obstruction to congruence must already live in the arithmetic of that single
cubic; the analytic input of the full conjecture should be replaceable, for the
non-existence direction, by a finite descent.

Why now? Databases of elliptic curves organized by conductor make it possible to test,
across thousands of curves `Eₙ`, whether a uniform bounded-modulus certificate tracks
non-congruence exactly, turning a structural hope into a falsifiable pattern.

## 2. Additivity of vanishing order forces a "no-cancellation" law

**Conjecture.** Whenever an arithmetic L-function factors as a product of two
independent pieces, the order of vanishing at the central point is *exactly* the sum of
the two orders, with **no** cancellation — and this rigidity extends to the leading
coefficients, which multiply. Consequently, a factor can lower the central rank of a
product only by literally contributing zero order, never by interfering destructively.

The key insight is that the order of vanishing behaves like a valuation on the
multiplicative monoid of central germs: the lowest surviving term of a Cauchy product is
a single, non-cancelling product of the two leading terms because the coefficient field
has no zero divisors.

Why now? Rankin–Selberg convolutions and Artin factorizations are being computed at
scale, so the additivity-with-no-cancellation prediction can be checked directly against
tables of central orders and leading terms for products of degree-1 and degree-2
objects.

## 3. Isogeny invariance pins down the Tate–Shafarevich order

**Conjecture.** Within an isogeny class, the quantity
`(real period) · (regulator) · (order of Ш) · (product of Tamagawa numbers) /
(order of torsion)²` is a class invariant, and this single constraint, combined with the
independently computable period, regulator, torsion and Tamagawa data, determines the
order of Ш for *every* curve in the class once it is known for one.

The key insight is that curves related by an isogeny share the same central leading
coefficient, so the entire arithmetic quotient above is forced to coincide across the
class; the mysterious factor `#Ш` is the only unknown and is therefore computable by
difference.

Why now? Complete isogeny classes with certified periods, regulators and Tamagawa
numbers are now tabulated, so the predicted cross-class equality of the arithmetic
quotient — and hence the derived values of `#Ш` — is immediately falsifiable.

## 4. A rank-zero dichotomy detectable from a single value

**Conjecture.** For an elliptic curve over the rationals, the Mordell–Weil group is
finite if and only if a single central special value is nonzero; moreover the "gap"
between that value being zero and nonzero is *quantized*: as one varies over curves of
bounded conductor, the nonzero central values do not accumulate at zero from above,
leaving a detectable spectral gap that separates rank-zero from higher-rank curves.

The key insight is that finiteness of the group is equivalent to non-vanishing of the
central value, so the rank-zero locus is cut out by one real equation; a quantitative
spectral gap would upgrade this qualitative criterion into an effective test.

Why now? High-precision central-value computations across large conductor ranges make it
feasible to measure the distribution of nonzero central values and search empirically for
the conjectured gap.

## 5. Squarefree scaling collapses the congruent-number problem to a density statement

**Conjecture.** Because congruence depends only on the squarefree part of `n`, the
congruent numbers have a *natural density among squarefree integers* equal to a simple
explicit constant, and the residues of congruent squarefree integers modulo `8` follow a
fixed proportion independent of any unproven analytic hypothesis.

The key insight is that scaling by a rational square preserves congruence, so the entire
problem descends to squarefree representatives, where the surviving structure is a clean
question of density rather than of individual membership.

Why now? Extensive tabulations of congruent numbers are available, so the predicted
density among squarefree integers and the residue proportions modulo `8` can be estimated
and stress-tested immediately.
